953.title: Genevieve (3 January)
953.hook: a young woman who calmed Paris during the siege of Attila
953.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Genevieve's memory in early January, especially in Paris, where she is honored as the city's patron and people pray for the city in her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was litany, a church full of names, each answered with pray for us. Your line was pray for us. Today the climb starts walking the calendar, saint by saint, in January.

Rumors arrive before armies do. In the story, word reaches Paris that Attila and his Huns are coming, burning cities on the way. People start loading carts: valuables wrapped in blankets, children on top, the city gates jammed. Neighbors shout advice across the street. Leaving seems like the only sane thing to do. And one young woman stands in the middle of the panic and says: stay. Don't run. Pray.
screen: `RUMORS ARRIVE BEFORE ARMIES.` → `CARTS AT THE CITY GATES.` → `ONE VOICE: STAY. PRAY.`

segments.voice: Genevieve lived in Paris in the days when Roman Gaul was coming apart. An early account of her life tells her story, and the Church remembers her in early January. She was a consecrated virgin: not a nun in a convent, but a woman who had given her life to God and lived it out in the city, praying, fasting and caring for people. When the news of Attila came, the account says, she gathered the women of Paris to pray, and she begged the men not to carry their goods away. The cities they fled to, she warned, would not be safe; Paris would be protected. That did not go down well. Some citizens called her a false prophet and, the account says, talked about stoning her or throwing her in the river. Then a churchman arrived from Auxerre, where the bishop Germanus had once praised her, and he spoke up for her, and the crowd backed off. And Attila's army turned away. It never reached Paris. Catholics honor Genevieve as the patron of Paris, and her story sits easily next to a line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it." What she did is ordinary and very hard. She didn't fight. She didn't flee. In a crowd that was spinning, she stayed still, prayed, and asked others to do the same. Calm can be contagious. So can panic. She chose which one to pass on.
screen: `A CONSECRATED WOMAN IN THE CITY.` · `STAY AND PRAY, WHEN EVERYONE RUNS.` · `THE CROWD TURNS ON HER.` · `THE ARMY TURNS AWAY.` · then, large: `UNLESS THE LORD KEEP THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Bring your own town to mind, not the whole map, just one street, one hospital, one bus stop, and whatever it's facing now: a storm, a shortage, a fear, a loss. Breathe slowly, the way Genevieve stood still. If you pray, ask God to keep your city, or ask Saint Genevieve to pray for it; if you don't, hold your city in mind calmly, without fixing anything.
Genevieve. A young woman of Paris who, in the story, urged the city to stay and pray when Attila's army came. Patron of Paris, remembered in early January.

954.title: Kuriakose Elias Chavara (3 January)
954.hook: a Syro-Malabar priest in Kerala who started schools for every parish
954.howItsDone: Syro-Malabar Catholics in Kerala and around the world honor Saint Kuriakose Elias Chavara in early January, especially at Mannanam, where he is buried, and in the schools and religious communities connected with him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Genevieve, who calmed Paris when everyone wanted to run. Your line was she calmed the city. Today, the same date on the calendar, the other side of the world.

In villages across Kerala, in the south of India, you can still find it: a church, and right next to it, a school. Children in uniforms run between the two at recess. The school bell and the church bell ring from almost the same spot. It looks so natural that nobody asks why. But that pairing didn't happen on its own. Someone asked for it, on purpose, parish by parish.
screen: `A CHURCH IN KERALA.` → `AND RIGHT BESIDE IT, A SCHOOL.` → `SOMEONE ASKED FOR IT, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Kuriakose Elias Chavara was a priest of the Syro-Malabar Church, one of the Eastern Catholic Churches, fully Catholic but with its own liturgy and customs. Its people trace their faith back, in their tradition, to the apostle Thomas. Chavara grew up in Kerala, was ordained, and gave his life to renewing that Church from the inside. He helped found a religious congregation of priests and brothers who would pray, preach and teach together. He set up a printing press so books could be made and read at home. He helped start a congregation of religious sisters too. And when he was given authority over the Syro-Malabar parishes, he asked that each parish have a school alongside its church, open to the children of the village. Why a school? For him, faith and learning belonged in the same place. A child who could read could read the Gospels, and also a contract, a letter, a newspaper. Catholics hear a line of Jesus about children in that work, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children, and forbid them not to come to me: for the kingdom of heaven is for such." Chavara also wrote a letter of advice to families, known as the Testament of a Loving Father, full of plain counsel about raising children, keeping the home peaceful and treating servants and neighbors well. Pope Francis declared him a saint. His legacy is easy to walk past: a building with desks, next to a building with an altar.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a teacher who changed something for you: the room, the desk, their face, the thing they made possible. If you pray, pray for them, and for the children in a school near you; if not, simply hold that teacher in mind with gratitude.

955.title: André Bessette (early January)
955.hook: a sickly doorkeeper in Montreal who welcomed thousands and built a shrine to Joseph
955.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint André Bessette in early January; pilgrims visit Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal, where he is buried, and some pray there with oil blessed in Saint Joseph's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kuriakose Elias Chavara, who wanted faith and learning in the same place. Your line was a school beside every church.

A knock at a school's front door in Montreal. A small, thin man in a religious habit opens it. He takes your coat, asks who you've come to see, and lets you wait by the stove. He does this all day. He sweeps the floor, runs errands, cuts the students' hair. He can barely read. His health was so poor that his religious order nearly sent him away. He later joked that his superiors showed him the door, and he stayed there.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR IN MONTREAL.` → `A THIN MAN TAKES YOUR COAT.` → `THEY SHOWED HIM THE DOOR. HE STAYED.`

segments.voice: André Bessette was a brother of the Congregation of Holy Cross in Quebec; people called him Brother André. He was weak from childhood, had little schooling, and worked odd jobs before he entered religious life. His community hesitated to keep him, but they did, and made him porter, the doorkeeper of their college in Montreal. A doorkeeper sees everyone: students, parents, the sick, the poor, the curious. André had a deep love for Saint Joseph, the quiet carpenter, and he began to pray with people who came to the door with troubles, especially the sick. He would encourage them to pray to Joseph, and sometimes rubbed them with oil from a lamp burning before Joseph's statue. People said they were healed. Crowds started coming to the door, then to a small wooden chapel he wanted built on the slope of Mount Royal. That chapel grew, over his lifetime and after it, into Saint Joseph's Oratory, a great basilica above the city. André never took the credit. He insisted it was Joseph, and God, who healed; he was only the one who opened the door. There's a psalm line he could have hung over his post, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have chosen to be an abject in the house of my God, rather than to dwell in the tabernacles of sinners." An abject is the lowliest person there; in some translations, a doorkeeper. Pope Benedict declared him a saint. The man they nearly sent away is buried in the shrine he started.

956.title: Marguerite Bourgeoys (12 January)
956.hook: a pioneer teacher in early Montreal, founder of an uncloistered community
956.howItsDone: Catholics remember Saint Marguerite Bourgeoys in January, especially in Montreal and in schools of the Congregation of Notre-Dame, whose sisters still teach and serve without a cloister.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brother André, the doorkeeper who said it was Joseph who healed. Your line was the doorkeeper. Today, Montreal again, back when it was barely a town.

A stone stable, empty of animals, swept out. A woman from France stands in it, looking at the walls. Outside is a tiny settlement on an island in a wide river: wooden houses, a fort, forest in every direction, winters she has never imagined. There are only a few children in the whole place. She is going to teach them anyway, here, in this stable. The settlement will become Montreal.
screen: `A STONE STABLE, SWEPT OUT.` → `A TINY SETTLEMENT IN THE FOREST.` → `SHE WILL TEACH HERE ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Marguerite Bourgeoys grew up in Troyes, in France. As a young woman she felt drawn to God, and to teaching, and she joined a group of laywomen who taught poor girls in her town. The governor of the little French settlement of Ville-Marie, on the island that would become Montreal, came looking for a teacher, and she crossed the ocean with him. In the settlement she was given a stone stable, and she opened a school in it. But she wanted more than one classroom. She wanted women who would teach wherever they were needed, and that raised a problem. In her day, the Church usually expected women's religious communities to be cloistered: enclosed behind walls, praying, not traveling. Marguerite took her model from Mary in the Gospel of Luke, who, after the angel's visit, went to help her cousin Elizabeth. In the Douay-Rheims: "And Mary rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Juda." A Mary who walked out the door. So her community, the Congregation of Notre-Dame, was uncloistered. Its sisters lived among the people, taught children, trained young women arriving from France to make homes in a hard new place, and went where the need was. Church authorities were cautious at first, and approval took patience. Saint John Paul the Second declared her a saint. She started with a stable and a handful of children.

957.title: Hilary of Poitiers (13 January)
957.hook: a married convert who searched his way into the Church, then took exile rather than sign
957.howItsDone: Catholics keep Hilary's memorial in January with the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, honoring him as a bishop and Doctor of the Church whose writing on the Trinity is still read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marguerite Bourgeoys, who taught in a stable in early Montreal. Your line was a teacher in the wilderness.

A grown man in Roman Gaul, comfortable, educated, with a household of his own, sits with his books and a question that won't leave him alone: what is a human life for? He has tried the philosophers. Eat well, rest well, live decently. It isn't enough. Then he opens the Jewish scriptures and reaches the burning bush, where Moses asks God's name and hears an answer that is barely a name at all. As a bishop, he will call that moment the turn of his life. His name was Hilary, and he would choose exile over a signature.
screen: `WHAT IS A LIFE FOR?` → `THE BURNING BUSH.` → `A BISHOP WHO WOULDN'T SIGN.`

segments.voice: Hilary tells his own story at the start of his book On the Trinity. God's words to Moses stopped him. In the Douay-Rheims: "I AM WHO AM." Nothing, he writes, could say more about God than that: God simply is. He read on into the Gospels and asked for baptism. Tradition says he already had a wife and a daughter. Later the people of Poitiers made this married convert their bishop. Then the argument arrived. Christians were fighting over whether the Son is truly God, as fully as the Father, or something a step lower. The Emperor favored the bishops who said a step lower, and leaned on the rest to go along and to condemn Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria who held that the Son is fully God. Hilary would not put his name to it. So he was sent far to the east, into exile. And there, cut off from his church, he wrote. On the Trinity starts from the words of baptism, at the close of Matthew's Gospel: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." His point is simple and stubborn: if that is the name you were baptized into, you don't get to quietly edit it later. Later he came home and kept teaching. Tradition says a man just out of the army came to learn from him, the one the Church remembers as Martin of Tours. The Church later named Hilary a Doctor of the Church. Steady, here, doesn't mean loud. It means the same answer on a good day and in exile.

958.title: Anthony the Abbot (17 January)
958.hook: the desert father who heard one Gospel line and walked out; patron of animals, blessed in villages on his day
958.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Anthony the Abbot's memorial in January, and in some places priests bless farm animals and pets on or near his feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hilary of Poitiers, who chose exile over condemning a fellow bishop. Your line was hilary the steady.

Two graves are fresh in an Egyptian village, and the young man who buried them was their son. He has land, a younger sister to look after, and a lot on his mind. One day he walks into church while the Gospel is being read, and the line, his biographer says, lands on him as if it were read for him alone. He walks out and starts giving his fields away. In some villages, on his feast in January, people still bring cows, horses, dogs and chickens to be blessed in his name.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN, NEWLY ORPHANED.` → `ONE GOSPEL LINE.` → `HE GIVES HIS FIELDS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Anthony's story comes to us through the Life of Antony, written by Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria we met yesterday. The line Anthony heard was Jesus speaking to the rich young man in Matthew's Gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor". Anthony did it. He kept a little back for his sister, Athanasius says, until he heard another line, about not being anxious for tomorrow, and gave that away too. He placed his sister with a community of faithful women and went out to live alone: first at the edge of his village, then among old tombs, then deep in the desert, inside an abandoned fort. He stayed a long time. Athanasius describes a real fight: temptations, fear, nights when he felt attacked. Then the surprise. People came looking for him. When he finally walked out, Athanasius says, his friends were amazed: he looked neither wasted nor overfed, and his mind was calm. Others moved into the desert near him to live the same way, and he taught them. That's why tradition calls him the father of monks. Now the animals. Athanasius tells how wild beasts kept trampling Anthony's little garden. He caught one gently and told them all, in effect, I do you no harm, so do me none, and leave. And they left. In time, Christians came to call on him as a patron of animals and farm creatures. So on his day: a priest with holy water in a village square, and a line of farm animals waiting their turn.

959.title: Sebastian (20 January)
959.hook: a soldier-martyr painted pierced with arrows, who in his story survives them; patron of athletes
959.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Sebastian's memorial in January, and sports clubs, athletes and soldiers in various places honor him as a patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony the Abbot, who heard one Gospel line and walked into the desert. Your line was the father of monks.

In a gallery of old paintings, a young man looks back at you, tied to a tree or a column, calm, with arrows standing out of his body. It's easy to assume you're looking at the moment he died. In his story, you aren't. The arrows are the part he survived. His name is Sebastian, and he ends a week of saints from the calendar's first weeks of January.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN AND THE ARROWS.` → `NOT THE MOMENT HE DIED.` → `WHAT CAME AFTER.`

segments.voice: Very little about Sebastian is certain. Saint Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, mentions him as a martyr from Milan who died in Rome. The full story comes from a much later account, and here is the story it tells, the one the Church has handed down. Sebastian was an officer in the emperor's guard and quietly a Christian. He used his post to visit Christians in prison and keep their courage up. When he was found out, the emperor had him tied up and shot with arrows by his own fellow soldiers, and left for dead. A Christian widow named Irene came at night to take his body for burial, and found him breathing. She took him home and nursed him. Then the turn. Healed, Sebastian did not leave Rome. He stood where the emperor would pass and told him to his face that he was wrong to persecute Christians. This time he was beaten to death. Tradition honors him as a patron of athletes and soldiers, and some readers see why: a body that took the blow and got back up. Some hear in him Paul's words near the end of his second letter to Timothy. In the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Look back at this week: Genevieve calming Paris, Kuriakose Chavara putting a school beside a church, André the doorkeeper, Marguerite teaching in a stable, Hilary refusing to sign, Anthony walking into the desert. And Sebastian, getting back up.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who trains their body: a kid at Saturday soccer, a friend who runs before work, someone learning to walk again after an injury. Picture them in the last stretch, the moment they want to stop. If you pray, ask Sebastian to pray for them; if you don't, wish them strength and a safe body, one name at a time.
